w: Ground broken in 1818 under Ferdinand VII, opened by his daughter Isabella II in 1850, shut for damage in 1925, resurrected as a concert hall in 1966, and not reopened as an opera house proper until 1997 after a six-year overhaul. Along the way it's hosted Eurovision, the Goya Awards and Spain's Christmas lottery draw.
s: An opera house that took 179 years to finish opening
_facts: Groundbreaking 23 April 1818 under Ferdinand VII; opened by Queen Isabella II on 19 November 1850
Closed 1925 due to building damage; reopened 1966 as a symphonic concert venue
Major refurbishment from 1991; reopened as an opera house 11 October 1997
Hosted the 1969 Eurovision Song Contest and the 2011 Goya Awards; hosts the Christmas Loteria Nacional draw since 2012

w: Spain's answer to Downing Street: the Prime Minister's official residence and workplace since 1977, when Adolfo Suarez moved in from the old Palace of Villamejor. It's really a compound - sixteen buildings, a hospital and a bunker - and the name alone now stands in for the whole central government.
s: The palace that became shorthand for the government
_facts: Official residence/workplace of the Prime Minister of Spain since 1977, relocated from the Palace of Villamejor by Adolfo Suarez
Part of the Moncloa Complex: 16 buildings, a bunker and a hospital
Houses the Ministry of the Presidency, Deputy PM's Office, Cabinet Office, Chief of Staff's Office and Press Office; weekly Council of Ministers meets there
'Moncloa' is used as a metonym for the Spanish central government

w: Anchoring the western end of the Gran Via, this square pairs a monument to Cervantes with two of Madrid's tallest skyscrapers looming over it. It spent two and a half years fenced off for renovation before reopening to pedestrians only, in November 2021.
s: Cervantes, skyscrapers and a two-year renovation
_facts: Large square at the western end of the Gran Via
Features a monument to Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra
Adjacent to two of Madrid's most prominent skyscrapers; the Royal Palace is a short walk south
Reopened for pedestrians 22 November 2021 after 2.5 years of renovation

w: Nicknamed the 'Spanish Broadway', this stretch from Calle de Alcala to Plaza de Espana reads like a catalogue of early-1900s revival styles - Vienna Secession jostling Plateresque and Neo-Mudejar facades. Its grand old cinemas have mostly been evicted for shopping centres since the late 2000s.
s: Madrid's Broadway, a museum of facades
_facts: Runs from Calle de Alcala (near Plaza de Cibeles) to Plaza de Espana
Nicknamed the 'Spanish Broadway'; major shopping street with hotels and large cinemas
Showcases early 20th-century revival architecture: Vienna Secession, Plateresque, Neo-Mudejar, Art Deco
Since the late 2000s many cinemas have been replaced by shopping centres

w: King Felipe VI's working palace, though the family's true official residence is the grander Royal Palace across town. Juan Carlos I lived here from 1962 until 2020, when allegations of financial impropriety sent him abroad - Queen Sofia stayed behind, and the king now lives next door in the Pabellon del Principe.
s: The palace a king left in disgrace
_facts: Working residence/office of King Felipe VI; the family's official residence is the Royal Palace of Madrid
Owned by the Spanish state, administered by Patrimonio Nacional
Home of King Juan Carlos I from May 1962 until he left Spain in August 2020 amid allegations of financial impropriety
Queen Sofia remained; Felipe VI has his office there but lives in the adjacent Pabellon del Principe

w: Leaning fifteen degrees off vertical, these twin towers were the first inclined skyscrapers built anywhere in the world - designed by Philip Johnson for the Kuwait Investment Office, hence the old nickname 'Torres KIO'. One rooftop helipad is outlined in blue, the other in red, like a mismatched pair.
s: The world's first skyscrapers built off-kilter
_facts: Twin office towers near Plaza de Castilla, 114m/26 floors, built 1989-1996
Each tower inclines 15 degrees - the first inclined skyscrapers in the world
Designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee; originally commissioned by the Kuwait Investment Office (nicknamed 'Torres KIO')
West tower's helipad is outlined in blue, the east tower's in red
